statements.markdown:
First consider a gap $(a,b)$ with both endpoints in $S$, allowing
$a=0$. Compact-strip regularity gives continuity of $q'$ on $[a,b]$,
even if $\gamma$ jumps at an endpoint. Contact gives
$$
q(a)=a,\qquad q(b)=b,\qquad q'(a),q'(b)\le1.
\tag{5.4}
$$
If the constant coefficient is $c>0$, Section 4 makes $q'$ strictly
convex in the gap. Continuity extends the chord comparison to its
endpoints, giving
$$
q'(t)<\frac{b-t}{b-a}q'(a)+\frac{t-a}{b-a}q'(b)\le1,
\qquad a<t<b.
\tag{5.5}
$$
Integrating contradicts $q(b)-q(a)=b-a$. Equivalently, the mean value
theorem applied to (5.4) requires an interior point with $q'=1$,
whereas (5.5) excludes every such point. The endpoint derivatives need
only be at most one; equality has not been assumed.

statements.markdown:
The sign of the contradiction is now explicit. For $s'$ sufficiently
close to one, the estimate holds at every $t\in[s',1)$, so
$$
\begin{aligned}
G(s')&=\int_{s'}^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\\
&\le\frac{(1-s')^2}{2}
       -\frac{2C}{3}(1-s')^{3/2}<0.
\end{aligned}
$$
The final inequality holds once $\sqrt{1-s'}<4C/3$. It contradicts
the nonnegative cost of adding an atom at $s'$. This proof covers
$c=0$ as well as $c>0$. In particular, empty support is impossible:
then $\mu_\gamma=0$ and $\gamma=0$ on all of $[0,1)$.

statements.markdown:
Fix $s\in(a,1)$ and let $\rho_s$ be the law of $X_s$. Choose
$R<\infty$ such that $p_0=\rho_s([-R,R])>0$. For $c>0$, set
$$
h(t,y)=\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt{1-t}Z|},\qquad
\Phi(t,y)=c^{-1}\log h(t,y),
$$
where $Z$ is standard normal. The drift on this interval is
$c\Phi_x=h_x/h$, and the transition density is
$$
k_{s,t}(x,y)=p_{t-s}(y-x)\frac{h(t,y)}{h(s,x)},\qquad
p_v(z)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/(2v)}.
\tag{5.2}
$$
The heat-semigroup identity normalises this kernel; equivalently, for
Brownian motion started at $(s,x)$, $h(t,B_t)/h(s,x)$ is the positive
mean-one change of measure which adds the drift $h_x/h$. For $c=0$,
the same kernel formula applies
with $h=1$, and the value function is the ordinary heat evolution of
$|x|$.

statements.markdown:
For the actual moment function associated with $\gamma$, the two
potential conditions $G\ge0$ and $G=0$ on $S$ are also sufficient for
minimality. This ordinary deduction explains exactly how much variational
information has been extracted. For another admissible coefficient
$\beta$, let $\nu=\mu_\beta$. The weighted identity above and
$|G(s)|\le1-s$ make both measure integrals absolutely convergent, even
when either measure has infinite total mass. Fubini gives
$$
2D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\beta-\gamma]
 =\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\nu(ds)
  -\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu(ds)\ge0.
$$
Here the second integral is zero because $\mu$ is concentrated on its
relative support. The control formula also shows that $\mathcal P$ is
convex in its coefficient: for a fixed control, the terminal absolute
value is convex in the coefficient and both penalties are linear; taking
the supremum over the same control class preserves convexity. Therefore
$$
\mathcal P(\beta)-\mathcal P(\gamma)
 \ge D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\beta-\gamma]\ge0.
$$
This proves the converse.
statements.note: Not in the Lean: only the forward direction exists. The converse and convexity of the Parisi functional in its coefficient have no declaration.
statements.section: 3.5 What the first-order criterion does, and does not, establish

statements.markdown:
**Proof.** Fix $t<T<T'<1$ and a shrinking interval
$[t-\delta_n,t+\delta_n)\subset(0,T)$. Approximate $\gamma$ by
$$
h_n=\max\{\epsilon_n,\min\{K_n,
                  \eta_n\lfloor\gamma/\eta_n\rfloor\}\},
$$
where $0<\epsilon_n<c<K_n$, $\epsilon_n,\eta_n\downarrow0$ and
$K_n\uparrow\infty$. Use $\min(c,h_n)$ to the left of the interval,
$c$ on it, and $\max(c,h_n)$ to its right. Monotonicity makes these
positive, nondecreasing, right-continuous finite-step coefficients
$\gamma_n$. Clipping toward $c$ outside the interval cannot increase
the error, and
$$
\|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_1
\le\epsilon_n+\eta_n+\int_0^1(\gamma-K_n)_+\,ds
 +2\delta_n\sup_{|s-t|\le\delta_n}|\gamma(s)-c|
 \longrightarrow0.
\tag{4.3}
$$
Integrability controls the capped tail and continuity at $t$ the last
term. Choose smooth terminal parameters $M_n\ge\max(n,K_n)$.
The terminal values then converge uniformly to $|x|$, and the coefficient
masses have a common bound. The finite-step inequality of §4.4 applies
at $t$, where every $\gamma_n$ equals the same positive $c$.
statements.note: Lean builds no plateau at t: it samples at grid times tending to t, and the height tends to c by continuity.
statements.section: 4.5 A fixed-time inequality and its plateau application

To obtain Lemma 2 for an integrable coefficient, choose positive
monotone step coefficients $\gamma_n$ retaining the plateau near a
fixed interior time, with $\|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_1\to0$, and terminal
parameters $M_n\geq\|\gamma_n\|_\infty$ with $M_n\to\infty$.
Spatial derivatives through order four converge uniformly on a fixed
strip below one, and the diffusions driven by the same Brownian
motion converge
(see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2 and Proposition 5.1][FS]). Only
$v,w,z$ remain in (5), so no convergence theorem for the auxiliary
logarithmic derivative $s$ is needed.

statements.markdown:
On a fixed strip containing $t$ and ending before one, compact-strip
regularity gives uniform spatial convergence and bounds through order
four. The next derivative bounds give a common spatial Lipschitz
constant for those derivatives. Coupling with the same Brownian motion
and applying Gronwall gives a deterministic bound
$\sup_{s\le T}|X_s^n-X_s|\to0$. If $D_k^n=\partial_x^k\Phi_n$
and $D_k=\partial_x^k\Phi$, then, for $1\le k\le4$,

$$
|D_k^n(t,X_t^n)-D_k(t,X_t)|
\le\|D_k^n-D_k\|_{\infty,[0,T]\times\mathbb R}
   +C_{k,T}|X_t^n-X_t|\longrightarrow0.
$$

statements.markdown:
For completeness, let $V,W,Z$ bound both the limiting and approximating
$v,w,z$, and let $e_v,e_w,e_z$ bound their coupled evaluation errors.
Uniform spatial convergence and the path bound above give these errors
with $e_v,e_w,e_z\to0$. Difference-of-powers identities give
$$
\begin{aligned}
|\mathbb E\mathcal C(v_n,w_n,z_n)-\mathbb E\mathcal C(v,w,z)|
 &\le(12W^2+24V^3)e_v+24VW e_w+2Ze_z,\\
|\mathbb E v_n^4-\mathbb E v^4|&\le4V^3e_v,
\end{aligned}
$$
where $\mathcal C(v,w,z)=z^2-12vw^2+6v^4$. These constants depend
on the common strip and coefficient mass bound, not on plateau width.
statements.note: Not in the Lean: it has no difference-of-powers bounds. Both limits pass by dominated convergence, so these constants do not appear.

Let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ be
constant with value $c$ on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$, and let $X$
be its diffusion started at zero. Then

$$
\begin{cases}
q'''(t)\ge \dfrac1{1000c^2}
  \mathbb E\bigl[(c\Phi_{xx}(t,X_t))^4\bigr]>0,&c>0,\\[4pt]
q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0,&c=0,
\end{cases}\qquad t\in I.
$$

Thus $q'$ is strictly convex for $c>0$ and strictly increasing for
$c=0$.

statements.markdown:
**Corollary 4.2 (positive plateaus).** Suppose now that $\gamma=c>0$
on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$ and $t\in I$. Then (4.2) gives
$q'''(t)=\mathcal C_\gamma(t)$. To establish strictness for this
limiting solution, choose $b\in I$ later than $t$ and put
$\psi=\Phi_\gamma(b,\cdot)$. This is smooth, convex, even and a
bounded distance from $|x|$, so $\psi'$ cannot be constant. The
Cole–Hopf formula gives

$$
\Phi_{xx}(t,x)
=\mathbb E^{\rm tilt}_{t,x}\psi''
  +c\operatorname{Var}^{\rm tilt}_{t,x}(\psi'),
$$
$$
\nu_{t,x}(dy)=
\frac{e^{c\psi(y)}p_{b-t}(y-x)}
 {\int_{\mathbb R}e^{c\psi(z)}p_{b-t}(z-x)\,dz}\,dy.
$$

The tilted density is positive everywhere. Its variance of the
nonconstant continuous function $\psi'$ is strictly positive; its
mean of $\psi''$ is nonnegative. Thus $v(t,x)>0$ for every $x$, and
$\mathbb E v(t,X_t)^4>0$. Combining the limiting inequality with
the differentiated identity proves
$q'''(t)\ge(1000c^2)^{-1}\mathbb E v(t,X_t)^4>0$.
This proves strict convexity of $q'$ on $I$.
statements.section: 4.5 A fixed-time inequality and its plateau application

statements.markdown:
The same pointwise obstruction occurs with the actual terminal datum
$|x|$. For the admissible constant coefficient $\gamma_c\equiv c>0$,
write $\tau=1-t>0$ and use the same heat formula:
$$
\Phi_c(t,x)=c^{-1}\log\mathbb E e^{c|x+\sqrt\tau Z|}.
$$
At $c=0$ its continuous extension is the heat value, whose derivatives are
$$
a_0=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi\tau}}e^{-x^2/(2\tau)},\qquad
b_0=-\frac{x}{\tau}a_0,\qquad
d_0=\left(\frac{x^2}{\tau^2}-\frac1\tau\right)a_0.
$$
At $x=\sqrt\tau$, $d_0=0$ and $b_0^2=a_0^2/\tau>0$.
For fixed $t,x$, Gaussian convolution may be differentiated in $x$
through its kernel and expanded in $c$ near zero: exponential moments
dominate every resulting polynomial factor. The apparent singularity
of $c^{-1}\log\mathbb E e^{c|x+\sqrt\tau Z|}$ is removable, and its
spatial derivatives through order four are smooth in $c$. Hence
$$
d_c^2-12c a_cb_c^2+6c^2a_c^4
 =-\frac{12a_0^3}{\tau}c+O(c^2)<0
$$
for all sufficiently small positive $c$, at that fixed point.

There is a concrete obstruction to reading the last display pointwise.
For the smooth finite-step problem $c=M=1$ on $[0,1)$, with terminal
value $\log(2\cosh x)$, the exact solution is

$$
\Phi(t,x)=\log(2\cosh x)+\frac{1-t}{2},\qquad r=\tanh x.

Indeed, $\Phi_{xx}+\Phi_x^2=1$. Writing $R=r^2$ gives
$v=1-R$, $w=-2rv$ and $z=-2v^2+4Rv$. At $R=1/2$,
$v=1/2$, $w^2=1/2$ and $z=1/2$, so

$$

$$

statements.markdown:
**Proposition 2.1 (compact-strip regularity).** For $\gamma\in\mathcal U$
and $0\le T<1$, the value has bounded, jointly continuous spatial derivatives
of every positive finite order on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$. If admissible
coefficients converge in $L^1$ and their smooth, even, convex, one-Lipschitz
terminal values converge uniformly to $|x|$, these spatial derivatives
converge uniformly on each such strip. The bounds depend on the derivative
order, the fixed strip and a common coefficient mass bound. Time derivatives need only exist
almost everywhere across coefficient jumps. On an open constant interval,
the heat formula supplies the additional time smoothness used in §4.
The terminal estimate is
$$
|x|\le\Phi_\gamma(t,x)
\le |x|+\sqrt{2(1-t)/\pi}+\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\,ds.
$$

statements.markdown:
First consider the value as a function of the starting state, holding
$t$ and $\gamma$ fixed; we also write $\Phi=\Phi_\gamma$.
For any permitted control, use the same
responses to each Brownian history at two starting states $x$ and $y$.
The costs are unchanged, and the triangle inequality bounds the change
in the terminal reward by $|x-y|$. Taking the supremum over controls gives

$$
|\Phi_\gamma(t,x)-\Phi_\gamma(t,y)|\le |x-y|.
$$

The value is also **convex**: between two states its graph lies at or
below the chord joining their values. Indeed,
each fixed-control payoff is an average of translated absolute-value
functions, hence convex. Its chord lies at or below the chord of the
best endpoint payoffs; taking the supremum preserves that upper bound.

statements.markdown:
Take $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=1$,
$0<c_1\le\cdots\le c_N\le M$, and
$\gamma(t)=c_i$ on $[t_{i-1},t_i)$. The terminal value is
$M^{-1}\log(2\cosh Mx)$. On a step of height $c$, set $l=c\Phi$ and
$h=e^l$. Then $h_t=-\tfrac12h_{xx}$. For $a<t$ in that step the
diffusion transition density is

$$
p_{t-a}(x-y)\frac{h(t,x)}{h(a,y)},\qquad
p_t(x)=(2\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(2t)}.
$$

Its mass is one by $h(a,\cdot)=P_{t-a}h(t,\cdot)$. Factoring the
positive-time density as $f=e^l g$ gives $g_t=\tfrac12g_{xx}$ on each
step. Put $s=-\partial_x\log g$. On the first step,
$g(t,x)=p_t(x)e^{-l(0,0)}$ and $s=x/t$. At a forward jump
$\delta=c_+-c_-\ge0$, continuity of $f$ gives
$g_+=g_-e^{-\delta\Phi}$. The functions $r$ and $s$ are odd.
statements.section: 4.2 The smooth finite-step problem and its boundary control

statements.markdown:
The comparison arguments take place on unbounded spatial domains, so
the boundary estimates must precede the signs. For these fixed smooth
data, Gaussian convolution and the finite jump rules give, as
$x\to+\infty$,

$$
l(t,x)=cx+C(t)+O(e^{-\kappa x}),
$$
$$
g(t,x)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2}{2t}+\beta(t)x+C_0(t)\right)
       (1+O(e^{-\kappa x})).
$$

The errors may be differentiated any fixed finite number of times;
the estimates are uniform on each closed step, with positive time
bounded away from zero for the forward estimate. Their constants may
depend on the step data. For example, after completing the square in a
Gaussian convolution, the error is an expectation at
$Y_x=\lambda x+b+\sqrt VZ$ with $\lambda$ bounded below by a positive
constant. Split at $Y_x=\mathbb EY_x/2$. The first part inherits the
exponential tail; on the second, the Gaussian probability dominates the
permitted exponential growth of the error and all its specified
derivatives. This proves the differentiated estimates by finite induction
through heat evolution and jumps. In particular,
$s=x/t-\beta(t)+O(e^{-\kappa x})$, $s_x=1/t+O(e^{-\kappa x})$ and
$s_{xx}=O(e^{-\kappa x})$.
statements.note: Not in the Lean: it has no tail expansions. The proof uses cruder exponential bounds against Gaussian decay.

statements.markdown:
Begin with a positive nondecreasing finite-step coefficient $\gamma_{\rm step}$: a function constant
on each interval of a finite partition. Replace the terminal value
$|x|$ by the smooth approximation $M^{-1}\log(2\cosh Mx)$, with
$M\geq\|\gamma_{\rm step}\|_\infty$.
On a step of height $c$, set $h=e^{c\Phi}$. Then
$h_t=-h_{xx}/2$ and $r=h_x/h$. The same exponential removes the
drift from the forward density equation. Indeed, writing $f=hg$ gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
f_t&=\tfrac12(hg)_{xx}-(h_xg)_x\\
   &=-\tfrac12h_{xx}g+\tfrac12hg_{xx}
    =h_tg+\tfrac12hg_{xx}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Comparison with $f_t=h_tg+hg_t$ yields $g_t=g_{xx}/2$.

statements.markdown:
Define the locally finite Stieltjes
measure by
$$
\mu_\gamma([0,t])=\gamma(t),\qquad 0\leq t<1.
$$
Thus $\mu_\gamma((s,t])=\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)$: the measure records
the increments of $\gamma$. A point mass (atom) of size $\gamma(0)$
is allowed at zero, and the total mass need not be finite or equal
to one. All support statements use the relative topology of $[0,1)$.

statements.markdown:
**Stieltjes measure** records the increments:

$$
\mu_\gamma([0,t])=\gamma(t),\qquad
\mu_\gamma((a,b])=\gamma(b)-\gamma(a).
$$

These cumulative values determine the measure uniquely. The first
equation permits mass $\gamma(0)$ at zero. Mass concentrated at one
point is an **atom**. The weights need not be probabilities of
finite-system overlaps, and their total need not be one or even finite.
They are finite on each $[0,T]$ with $T<1$.

finite example: place weight two at scale $1/4$ and weight one at scale

\begin{cases}

2,&1/4\le t<3/4,\\
3,&3/4\le t<1.
\end{cases}

statements.markdown:
Here is the elementary calculus step. Suppose
$q\in C^1([r,1))$, $q(r)=r$, $q'(r)\le1$, $q\le1$, and $q'$
is strictly convex on $(r,1)$. If $q(t)\ge t$ at some $r<t<1$,
strict integration below the finite endpoint chord gives
$$
t-r\le\int_r^t q'(v)\,dv
 <\frac{t-r}{2}\bigl(q'(r)+q'(t)\bigr),
$$
so $q'(t)>1$. For $t<s<1$, convexity then gives
$$
q'(s)\ge q'(t)+\frac{s-t}{t-r}\bigl(q'(t)-q'(r)\bigr)
\ge q'(t)>1.
$$
Consequently $q(s)\ge t+(s-t)q'(t)>1$ for $s$ sufficiently
close to one, a contradiction. Thus $q(t)<t$ throughout $(r,1)$.
All chord endpoints lie below one; no derivative at one is used.

statements.markdown:
A terminal gap $(r,1)$ with nonempty support has $r\in S$ and
positive plateau height. Suppose $q(t)\geq t$ for some $r<t<1$.
Strict convexity of $q'$ and $q'(r)\leq1$ give
$$
t-r\leq\int_r^t q'(s)\,ds
<\frac{t-r}{2}\bigl(q'(r)+q'(t)\bigr),
$$
so $q'(t)>1$. Convexity then gives $q'(s)>q'(t)>1$ for $s>t$.
Consequently $q(s)>t+(s-t)q'(t)>1$ for $s<1$ sufficiently
close to one, contrary to $q\leq1$. Thus $q(t)<t$ on $(r,1)$,
and $G(r)<0$ contradicts minimality. This uses no contact at one.
statements.section: 2. Minimality gives contact; curvature excludes gaps

statements.markdown:
**Reaching the diagonal forces a slope above one.**
Put $h(t)=q'(t)-1$, so $h(r)\le0$. If $q(t)\ge t$ at some
$r<t<1$, strict integration below the chord on the finite interval
$[r,t]$ would give

$$
0\le q(t)-t=\int_r^t h(v)\,dv
<\frac{t-r}{2}\bigl(h(r)+h(t)\bigr)
\le\frac{t-r}{2}h(t).
$$

Hence $h(t)>0$.

**The excess slope persists and violates the bound.**
To control a later slope, use the same chord rule
on the larger interval $[r,s]$, where $t<s<1$. At its interior
point $t$ this gives

$$
h(t)\le\frac{s-t}{s-r}h(r)+\frac{t-r}{s-r}h(s).
$$

Solving for the right endpoint gives

$$
h(s)\ge h(t)+\frac{s-t}{t-r}\bigl(h(t)-h(r)\bigr)\ge h(t)>0.
$$

The bound holds at every time after $t$, so integration gives
$q(s)\ge t+(s-t)(1+h(t))$. Choose any time

$$
t+\frac{1-t}{1+h(t)}<s<1.
$$

Such a choice exists because $h(t)>0$, and the lower bound now gives
$q(s)>1$, contradicting $q(s)\le1$ strictly before time one.
Thus $q(t)<t$ throughout $(r,1)$, giving
$G(r)=\int_r^1(q(t)-t)\,dt<0$, contrary to the addition test.

**[Question 4](#question-4).** Set $h=q'-1$. Since $q(r)=r$, reaching or passing the diagonal at
$t$ means $\int_r^t h\ge0$. Strict convexity places $h$ below its
endpoint chord, so that integral is less than

at least $h(t)$. Integrating gives
$q(s)\ge t+(s-t)(1+h(t))>1$ for a suitable $s<1$, violating the
bound. If $q$ never reaches the diagonal, then $G(r)<0$ instead.
Thus both possibilities contradict the conditions on a minimiser.

$c\ge0$ is finite. The endpoint $1$ is outside the support domain, so
there is no contact condition there to complete an endpoint-chord
argument. Instead we will prove
$$
1-q(t)\ge C\sqrt{1-t}
\tag{5.1}

statements.markdown:
Now write $\varepsilon=1-t$ and restrict to
$|y|\le\sqrt\varepsilon$. Differentiating the terminal heat formula
gives, with the unweighted interpretation for $c=0$,
$$
u(t,y)=
\frac{\mathbb E[\operatorname{sgn}(y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z)
                     e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}]}
     {\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}}.
$$
The denominator is at most
$D=e^c\mathbb E e^{c|Z|}<\infty$. Each sign has unnormalised
mass at least $p_*:=\mathbb P(Z\ge1)>0$: the threshold
$|y/\sqrt\varepsilon|$ is at most one, and the exponential weight
is at least one. Hence each sign has tilted probability at least
$\theta=p_*/D\in(0,1/2)$. It follows that
$$
|u(t,y)|\le1-2\theta,\qquad
1-u(t,y)^2\ge4\theta(1-\theta)=:\kappa>0.
$$
Multiplying this uniform deficit by the density lower bound (5.3)
and the window width $2\sqrt\varepsilon$ yields
$$
1-q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}(1-u(t,y)^2)f_t(y)\,dy
\ge 2m\kappa\sqrt{1-t}.
$$
This proves (5.1) with $C=2m\kappa$.

statements.markdown:
The admissible coefficient $\gamma_0=0$ makes the use of minimality in
the normalization step explicit. Its diffusion is $X_t=B_t$, and the
[zero-coefficient heat formula][fs-reg] gives

$$
u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1,
\qquad
a_0(t,x)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac{e^{-x^2/(2(1-t))}}{\sqrt{1-t}}.
$$

Since $\mathbb E e^{-\lambda B_t^2}=(1+2\lambda t)^{-1/2}$,

$$
\mathbb E a_0(t,B_t)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi},\qquad
\mathbb E a_0(t,B_t)^2=\frac2{\pi\sqrt{1-t^2}},\qquad
q_0(t)=\frac2\pi\arcsin t.
$$

The last identity follows by integrating $q_0'=\mathbb E a_0^2$
from $q_0(0)=0$. This heat and late-step variation argument is the
zero-field specialization of [Chen, Handschy and Lerman, Theorem 6
and its proof, arXiv:1609.04368v4, pp. 13–16](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4).
Strict convexity of $\arcsin$ gives $q_0(t)<t$
for $0<t<1$. Thus $G_0(s)=\int_s^1(q_0(t)-t)\,dt<0$ for
every $s<1$. Inserting an atom at $s$ is admissible, and its
[first variation][fs-var] is $G_0(s)/2<0$. In particular, the derivative for inserting
mass at zero is $1/4-1/\pi<0$. Hence this coefficient does not
minimize.

statements.markdown:
Return to the Gaussian value and slope from Section 3. With $\gamma=0$,
the state is $B_t$. Differentiating the slope once more gives

$$
X_t=B_t,\qquad
u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1,
\qquad
a_0(t,x)=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi(1-t)}}e^{-x^2/(2(1-t))}.
$$

A Gaussian integral gives
$\mathbb E e^{-B_t^2/(1-t)}=\sqrt{(1-t)/(1+t)}$. Substituting
into $q_0'=\mathbb E[a_0(t,B_t)^2]$ and integrating from zero yields

$$
q_0'(t)=\frac2{\pi\sqrt{1-t^2}},\qquad
q_0(t)=\frac2\pi\arcsin t.
$$

This recovers the half-time value $1/3$. It also shows that
$q_0(t)\to1$ while $q_0'(t)\to\infty$: convergence of a function
at one does not bound its derivative there.
The constant direction $\eta=1$ is admissible and adds an atom at zero.
Its cost is

$$
D\mathcal P(0)[1]
=\frac12\int_0^1\left(\frac2\pi\arcsin t-t\right)dt
=\frac14-\frac1\pi<0.
$$

So a small positive constant coefficient improves the zero candidate.

statements.markdown:
**A calculation at half time.** For $\gamma=0$, $X_t=B_t$ and
$B_{1/2}$ has the same distribution as $Z/\sqrt2$. We can average
over paths by grouping them according to the state reached. At half
time the reached state has density $e^{-x^2}/\sqrt\pi$. This density
describes its **law**, assigning probability to positions on the real line. The law has
total mass one even though the order-parameter measure $\mu_0$ is
zero. The two measures describe different objects.

statements.markdown:
Average $u_0(1/2,x)^2$ with this density. Substituting $x=z/\sqrt2$
gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_0(1/2)
&=\int_{\mathbb R}(2F_{\mathrm G}(z)-1)^2\varphi(z)\,dz\\
&=\int_0^1(2v-1)^2\,dv=\frac13,
\qquad v=F_{\mathrm G}(z),\quad dv=\varphi(z)\,dz.
\end{aligned}
$$

optimal at $\gamma=0$, $q_0$ uses the value slope $u_0$.
Section 7.1 uses the whole curve to find a feasible decrease of
$\mathcal P(0)$; a discrepancy at one time does not suffice.

but now set $t=1/4$. What variance has the state accumulated, and
what variance remains in its future reward? Write the Gaussian integral
for $q_0(1/4)$ without evaluating it.

statements.markdown:
**[Question 2](#question-2).** For $\gamma=0$, the state is $X_{1/4}=B_{1/4}$, a
centred Gaussian with variance $1/4$, so it has the law of $Z/2$.
The remaining independent Gaussian noise $B_1-B_{1/4}$ has variance
$3/4$ and standard deviation $\sqrt3/2$.
Thus

$$
q_0(1/4)=\int_{\mathbb R}
\left(2F_{\mathrm G}(z/\sqrt3)-1\right)^2\varphi(z)\,dz.
$$

The two variances agree at half time, but not here. For nonzero $z$,
the magnitude of the response is now smaller, so $q_0(1/4)<1/3$.
The arcsine formula in Section 7.1 also gives this comparison.

When $c=0$, the heat equation gives
$q''(t)=\mathbb E\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2$ without division by $c$.
Start the drift-free evolution at an earlier point of $I$; its
Gaussian transition kernel makes the law of $X_t$ have a positive
density everywhere. If the expectation were zero, continuity would
force $\Phi_{xxx}(t,\cdot)\equiv0$. Then $\Phi(t,\cdot)$ would
be an even quadratic polynomial. Its one-Lipschitz bound forces that
polynomial to be constant, contradicting its bounded distance from
$|x|$. Therefore $q''(t)>0$, giving strict increase of $q'$.

statements.markdown:
Here is why the inequality is strict. On this interval $X_t=B_t$,
whose density is positive everywhere at positive times. If the expected
square were zero, continuity would force $\Phi_{xxx}(t,x)=0$ for
every $x$: a nonzero value would give a small interval on which the
square is positive, and that interval has positive probability.
Then $\Phi(t,\cdot)$ would be a quadratic polynomial, and its bounded
slope would make it affine, a linear function plus a constant.
But choosing zero control gives
$\Phi_\gamma(t,x)\ge\mathbb E|x+B_1-B_t|\ge|x|$: the average
absolute value is at least the absolute value of the average. This
rules out an affine value: domination of $|x|$ in the positive tail
requires slope at least one, while the negative tail requires slope
at most minus one.
